title: Java
summary: A strongly typed, object-oriented language that runs enterprise systems and Android apps.

lessons.title: Java: syntax basics

concept.text:
Java is a **statically typed**, compiled language: every variable has a declared type, and the compiler checks your code before it ever runs. That catches many bugs early, at the cost of more typing.

All Java code lives inside a class, and a program starts at a method called `main`.
concept.analogy: Python is a chat with a friend: quick and informal. Java is a legal contract: everything is spelled out up front, which is slower to write but leaves far less room for surprises.

visual.caption: From source code to a running program.

steps.title: Declare typed variables
steps.text: State the type first. Statements end with a semicolon.

steps.title: Print
steps.text: `System.out.println` writes a line. `+` joins text and values.

steps.title: Branch and loop
steps.text: Blocks use curly braces. The classic for loop has a start, a condition and a step.

steps.title: Compile and run
steps.text: Install a JDK, then compile and run from a terminal.

challenge.prompt: Write a `main` method that adds up the numbers 1 to 100 using a loop and prints `Sum: 5050`.
challenge.hint: Declare `int sum = 0;` before the loop and add `i` to it each time round.

takeaways: Java is statically typed: declare the type of every variable.
Code lives in classes and starts at public static void main.
javac compiles to bytecode and the JVM runs it anywhere.

lessons.title: Java: classes, objects and collections

concept.text:
Java is object-oriented. A **class** is a blueprint that bundles data (fields) with behaviour (methods). An **object** is one thing built from that blueprint. **Encapsulation** means keeping fields private and exposing only safe methods.

For groups of objects, use collections: `ArrayList` for an ordered list and `HashMap` for key to value lookups.
concept.analogy: A class is a cookie cutter and objects are the cookies. One cutter, many cookies, each with its own icing (field values).

visual.caption: The four pillars of object-oriented programming.

items.title: Encapsulation
items.text: Hide data behind methods so it cannot be misused.

items.title: Inheritance
items.text: A class extends another and reuses its code.

items.title: Polymorphism
items.text: Different classes respond to the same method call in their own way.

items.title: Abstraction
items.text: Expose what something does, hide how it does it.

steps.title: Define a class
steps.text: The constructor runs when you create an object with `new`.

steps.title: Create objects
steps.text: Each object keeps its own balance.

steps.title: Use collections
steps.text: The type in angle brackets says what the collection holds.

steps.title: Extend a class
steps.text: A subclass inherits everything and can override methods.

challenge.prompt: Add a `withdraw(double amount)` method to `Account` that refuses to let the balance go below zero. It should return `true` if the withdrawal happened and `false` otherwise.
challenge.hint: Check `amount > balance` first and return false. This is encapsulation doing its job: the rule lives in one place.

takeaways: A class is a blueprint and an object is an instance made with new.
Keep fields private and enforce rules in methods.
ArrayList and HashMap cover most collection needs.

lessons.title: Java mini project: a grade book

concept.text: Combine classes and collections into a small grade book: students have a name and a list of scores, and the program reports each average and the top student. This is the shape of countless business programs: model the things, store them, loop and summarise.
concept.analogy: You are building a digital register: one card per student (object), kept in a box (list), with a method that works out each card's average.

steps.title: Model a student
steps.text: Give the class a method that computes its own average, so the logic lives with the data.

steps.title: Fill a list
steps.text: `List.of(...)` creates a fixed list of scores quickly.

steps.title: Report
steps.text: Loop once, printing each average with `printf` and remembering the highest so far.

interactive.expected:
Ava: 91.0
Ben: 72.0
Cy: 86.3
Top student: Ava

challenge.prompt: Add a `letterGrade()` method to `Student` that returns `"A"` for an average of 90 or more, `"B"` for 80 or more, `"C"` for 70 or more, and `"F"` otherwise.
challenge.hint: Call `average()` once, store it, then use an if / else if chain from highest to lowest.

takeaways: Put behaviour next to the data it uses.
Lists of objects plus a loop solve most reporting tasks.
printf formats numbers: %.1f means one decimal place.
